author: Climate Cosmos Team
title: Giant Hail Claims Life of 21-Year-Old Emu at Springfield's Dickerson Park Zoo - NewsBreak
text:
By Climate Cosmos Team ,
1 hours ago
The Storm’s Sudden Fury (Image Credits: Unsplash)
Springfield, Missouri – A ferocious hailstorm battered Dickerson Park Zoo on April 28, claiming the life of a longtime resident emu and injuring another animal amid widespread destruction. [1] [2] The storm, which struck around 11 a.m., forced staff to scramble for cover as softball-sized hail pelted the grounds. No humans were harmed, but the zoo shut down operations to assess the extensive damage.
The Storm’s Sudden Fury Keepers at Dickerson Park Zoo had just begun ushering animals into shelters when the supercell thunderstorm unleashed its payload. Hailstones measuring up to 4.75 inches across – comparable to softballs – rained down with ferocious intensity. [2] The onslaught lasted long enough to shred roofs and scatter debris across pathways.
Mark Burchfield, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Springfield, described the event as causing significant damage to vehicles and homes throughout the region. Former NOAA meteorologist Alan Gerard noted that such large hail arises when supercells split, with the left-moving branch favoring outsized ice chunks. [2] Local resident Lesa Voss captured the terror, telling KY3, “I’d never seen anything like that in my life. It’s the worst hail I have ever seen.”
Tragic Loss Among the Flightless Birds The zoo mourned the passing of Adam, a 21-year-old female emu who succumbed to injuries from the hail. Emus, native to Australia, often shelter by lying flat during threats, a behavior staff observed during the chaos. [3] A 17-year-old male rhea named Oscar also sustained head trauma and received veterinary treatment along with pain medication.
Joey Powell, the zoo’s public relations and marketing director, recounted the frantic response. “They immediately started getting animals put into shelters. And, you know, we took shelter as well and watched a hailstorm like we hope to never see again,” she said. [3] All other animals emerged unscathed, thanks to swift action by the team.
Damage Tallies and Road to Recovery Beyond the animal casualties, the hail tore through skylights, dented vehicles – including the zoo’s spay and neuter bus – and crumpled roofs at the adjacent Humane Society of Southwest Missouri. Debris littered walkways, prompting a full closure through April 29 as crews cleared paths and evaluated hidden structural issues. [3]
Powell emphasized safety priorities: “A lot of the damage is hidden. It’s out of sight, but you can see the debris on the paths, and that’s the focus now is to get that cleaned up so it’s safe for our guests to return.” The facility targeted a Friday reopening to host a Route 66 event, with volunteers aiding cleanup efforts.
Key Storm Impacts:
Hail size: 2-4.75 inches One emu fatality (Adam, 21 years old) One rhea injured (Oscar, head trauma) Damaged roofs, vehicles, skylights No staff or guest injuries Wider Repercussions and Weather Warnings The tempest extended far beyond the zoo, grounding flights at Springfield-Branson National Airport, shattering hundreds of car windshields, and sparking power outages for thousands. City utilities reported over a dozen gas meters struck, raising leak concerns. [2]
While Gerard called the hail unusual for late April, he stressed it fits Missouri’s volatile spring patterns. Recent studies link rising temperatures to intensified hail events, though more data is needed on global trends. As cleanup continues, the incident serves as a stark reminder of nature’s raw power in an era of shifting extremes.
Dickerson Park Zoo staff now focuses on healing – for animals and infrastructure alike – while the community reckons with the storm’s scars.
